title: Writing Reproducible and Testable Code
markdown:
## What this covers

Stat 243 is a computing course, and its second problem set is where the course stops teaching
bash and Python/R as separate topics and starts insisting they be used *together*, defensibly.
This chapter distills the recurring technical lessons behind that assignment as it was set in
three offerings — Fall 2021, Fall 2024 and Fall 2025 — rather than reproducing any one year's
instructions verbatim: how to make a shell pipeline reproducible by someone other than its author,
how to make a bash function behave like a well-mannered command-line tool, how to mix
languages inside one dynamic document, and how to turn a script that merely works into a module
that documents, defends and tests itself. It assumes a first-pass solution already exists — the
data-fetching code from Problem Set 1 — and basic fluency in bash and in Python or R.

## Reproducibility as a discipline, not a report

The instructions in every year make the same demand in the same words: you are not allowed to
narrate what you did ("I downloaded the data from such-and-such site, then unzipped it"); you have
to *give the commands* that would let someone else redo it. The Fall 2025 version sharpens this
into "the bash code that someone else could run to repeat what you did" — the test is not "can I
remember how I did this" but "can a stranger, or you in six months, replay it exactly."

That has a concrete consequence for how a solution is organized: every step that is normally done
by hand — downloading a file, unzipping an archive, subsetting a column — has to be expressed as a
line of shell that could be pasted into a fresh terminal and rerun. Anything typed in "by looking
at the file and copying the value" (a station ID, an item code) has to instead be looked up
*programmatically*, from the data itself, so that the pipeline still works if the file changes.

The Fall 2021 formatting requirements add the other half of reproducibility, the human-readable
half: a solution is not just code. It needs prose explaining the approach, and comments on each
function or non-obvious block, precisely because a script that runs correctly but explains nothing
is only reproducible by a machine, not by the next reader.

## One document, two languages: why the chunk "engine" matters

Both the Quarto documents (`.qmd`, 2024–2025) and the older R Markdown / LaTeX+knitr documents
(`.Rmd` / `.Rtex`, 2021) let a single file hold chunks of code in more than one language. All three
years hit the same underlying problem: the *engine* that executes those chunks is usually tied to
a single interpreter. Quarto's default `jupyter` engine assumes one Jupyter kernel per document,
and a kernel speaks one language — so a document with both a bash chunk and a Python chunk simply
cannot run both under `jupyter`.

The fix used in the course is to set `engine: knitr` in the document's YAML header. R's `knitr`
package dispatches each chunk to whatever language it declares, chunk by chunk, rather than
committing the whole document to one kernel — and it hands Python chunks to R's `reticulate`
package to actually execute. The consequence worth noticing: this means a Python-and-bash document
still needs R and the `knitr` package installed, purely to act as the traffic director between
chunks.

This machinery is flagged as unreliable enough to test in isolation, in both 2024 and 2025:
build a small dummy document with one bash chunk and one Python chunk before touching the real
problem set, since behavior — especially on Windows — is not guaranteed. If it does not work, the
year's fallback is to run the code on the department's shared machines instead of a laptop, or, as
a last resort, run the Python chunk separately and paste its output figure in by hand.

The 2021 version of the same problem, one tool generation earlier, is the same complaint about
bash chunks inside R Markdown / knitr documents (rather than about Python chunks inside Quarto):
troublesome especially on Windows, with three ad hoc fixes offered — switch the terminal to the
Ubuntu subsystem, turn on RStudio's notebook mode, or change single quotes to double quotes in the
document. The specific engines changed across the years; the underlying issue — a document that
mixes languages is fighting the tool's assumption that one document means one interpreter — did
not.

## Quoting: protecting an argument from the shell

A second theme surfaces independently in the bash-function exercise and in the data-download
exercise, and is worth stating once as a general rule rather than twice as two coincidences: a
value handed to the shell has to be quoted whenever it might contain something the shell would
otherwise try to interpret.

Inside an `if`, testing a variable against a string needs the variable in quotes:

```bash
if [ "${var}" == "some string" ]
if [ "${var}" != "some string" ]
```

The quotes matter because without them, a value containing a space, or a character the shell
treats as syntax, gets split into pieces or parsed as something other than plain text — exactly
the failure a defensive shell function is supposed to avoid.

The same principle shows up when constructing a URL to download from the command line: a query
string built from several parameters joined by `&` needs to be quoted, because an unquoted `&` is
itself shell syntax (it backgrounds a command). A URL copied out of a PDF can also pick up a stray
line break in the process, which silently breaks it in the same way — worth checking for before
concluding the quoting was the problem.

## A recurring headache: delimiters that appear inside the data

One further shell lesson worth recording on its own: a text format's delimiter is only useful if it
does not appear inside the data. A CSV file whose fields are, in general, comma-separated but which
also contains commas *inside* quoted character-string fields cannot be split reliably on `,` with
simple tools like `cut`. The practical fix is to convert the file to a different delimiter first —
done from the command line directly, or by shelling out to a one-line `Rscript` or Python
invocation to do the conversion — before the rest of the pipeline treats it as field-delimited
text.

## Designing a shell function as a small command-line program

Several years of the assignment ask for the same object: a bash *function* that wraps a small
download-and-process pipeline and is expected to behave the way a proper command-line tool would,
not just the way a script that happens to work does. Concretely, that means:

- **Validate its own arguments.** If the caller passes the wrong number of arguments, or a string
  that does not identify a single station, item or location, the function should say so with a
  useful message rather than fail deep inside the pipeline with an unrelated error.
- **Support a help flag.** Invoking the function as `get_weather -h` (or `myfun -h`) should print
  usage information, the same convention a real command-line tool follows.
- **Clean up after itself.** Raw downloaded files should either be deleted once the function is
  done with them, or downloaded into the operating system's temporary-file location in the first
  place, so that running the function repeatedly does not litter the working directory.
- **Keep its output pipeable.** The 2021 version is explicit that the function should print its
  result to `stdout` "such that the information could be piped to another UNIX command" — meaning
  status messages and progress information do not belong mixed into the same stream as the data.
  The Fall 2025 comments make the same point from the other direction, asking that a related part
  of the assignment print *only* the requested counts and avoid printing anything else, including
  download progress.

## From a script that works to a module that can be trusted

A second exercise, present in every year, does not ask for new code at all: it asks that a
solution to *Problem Set 1* — a first-pass function that already works — be hardened along three
axes. This is deliberately positioned as revision rather than fresh work, and each year's
instructions explicitly permit using an updated version of the PS1 solution if a bug in it came to
light from the reference solution or from talking to other students.

**Documentation.** Every function gets an informative docstring. Fall 2025 splits this into two
tiers: user-facing functions get a full docstring with a worked example, while internal helper
functions — the ones no caller outside the module is meant to invoke directly — get a more basic
one. The distinction tracks who the docstring is actually for: a user deciding how to call the
function, versus another developer reading the implementation.

**Defensive error handling.** The instructions ask for two different families of technique
depending on the language. In Python, that means exceptions: catching the ways a call can fail —
bad input from a user, but also external failures such as a server refusing the request or the
machine being offline — and, case by case, deciding whether the right response is to `raise` (stop,
and say why) or to catch the error with `try`/`except` and return `None` (fail quietly and let the
caller continue). Fall 2025 adds a third case worth keeping distinct from the other two: if the
external data itself is malformed — a JSON response whose keys or structure are not quite what was
expected — the recommended response is neither to crash nor to silently swallow the problem, but to
issue a *warning* and continue, since the result may still be partly usable. In R (2021), the same
idea is split into two separate library-backed tools: the `assertthat` package for run-time
assertions written into the code itself, checking inputs and conditions as execution proceeds.

**Testing.** A "thoughtful" — not exhaustive — set of unit tests, written with the language's
standard testing package: `pytest` in Python (2024, 2025), `testthat` in R (2021). The instructions
in 2021 frame the design question directly: think about the tricky cases that might actually cause
problems, rather than testing only the cases that are guaranteed to succeed.

## Reproducibility of someone else's research

Fall 2021 pairs the technical exercise above with a critical one that the later years drop: read
one of several assigned pieces on reproducible research practice, then apply the resulting
standard to a real published analysis rather than to your own code. The exercise gives a concrete
framework for what "reproducible" means for a finished project, distinct from "gives the same
answer": given a paper and its accompanying code repository, without reading either in depth, can
you quickly tell *where in the code* each of four stages happened — data collection, data cleaning,
computing the reported statistics, and producing the paper's plots — and can you tell what each
file and each block of code is for, just from documentation, naming, comments and organization,
without examining it closely? A project's reproducibility, on this standard, is measured by how
quickly a stranger can locate the answers to those questions, not by whether the numbers rerun.

## Exercises

**1. The Death Valley wedding problem (Fall 2024 / Fall 2025).** A wedding is being planned for
Death Valley National Park in March; the goal is to hold it as late in the month as possible
without a high chance of a very hot day. Using yearly station data from the Global Historical
Climatology Network, and working entirely from shell commands saved in the solution file (no
step done "by hand"):

  a. Download yearly climate data for a small, deliberately limited set of years into a temporary
     directory, printing to `stdout` the number of observations found for each year — including
     years with none — and nothing else (no download progress).
  b. Identify the Death Valley station programmatically from the network's `ghcnd-stations.txt`
     file (never by typing in its ID by hand), and subset the yearly files to that station, the
     `TMAX` variable, and the month of March, combining the result into a single file.
  c. In a Python or R chunk, using the single file from (b), produce one plot of side-by-side
     boxplots of the daily March maximum temperatures, one box per calendar day.
  d. Generalize (a) and (b) into a bash function taking a location string, a weather variable, and
     a time period (years and month) as arguments, and returning the corresponding results. The
     function should reject a wrong number of arguments, or an identifying string that does not
     resolve to a single station, with a useful error message; support `get_weather -h` for usage
     help; and remove the raw files it downloads (or download to a temporary location) rather than
     leaving them behind.

**2. Hardening the Problem Set 1 solution (Fall 2024 / Fall 2025).** Take the data-fetching
function(s) from Problem Set 1 (revised if needed) and add:

  a. Informative docstrings — with a worked example for each user-facing function, and at least a
     basic docstring for internal ones.
  b. Exception handling for the ways a call can fail, including inputs a user could get wrong and
     external failures such as an offline machine or a refused request; decide, case by case,
     whether to raise an exception or catch it and return `None`. Consider what should happen if
     the structure of a downloaded result (e.g., a JSON record) is not quite what the code expects.
  c. A thoughtful set of unit tests using `pytest`.

**3. Assertions and tests for the Problem Set 1 solution (Fall 2021, R).** For the same kind of
Problem Set 1 code, but in R:

  a. Add run-time assertions using the `assertthat` package, aimed at the various ways a user could
     misuse the function and at external failures (e.g., not being online).
  b. Write a small but carefully chosen set of tests with `testthat`, aimed at the tricky cases
     most likely to break something, not only the easy ones.

**4. Agricultural production data from the shell (Fall 2021).** The UN Food and Agriculture
Organization publishes crop production data downloadable via a direct URL that encodes an item
code (e.g., 526 for apricots) as a GET parameter.

  a. Using the shell, download the apricot data, strip out the metadata and the global-total row
     into a separate file, and subset to the year 2005 to find the ten regions using the most land
     (by area harvested) to grow apricots. Then automate the same analysis to report the top five
     regions for each of 1965, 1975, 1985, 1995 and 2005 — without repeating the code once per year
     — using only shell commands saved in the solution.
  b. Write a bash function that takes a single item code as its argument, downloads the
     corresponding data, and prints the resulting CSV to `stdout` in a form that could be piped to
     another Unix command. It should reject a wrong number of arguments with a useful message, and
     support a `-h` help flag.

**5. Reading and case study on reproducible research (Fall 2021).** In preparation for a section
discussion on reproducible research practice:

  a. Read one of a short list of assigned pieces on reproducibility (aimed variously at social
     science and at scientific computing generally), and write a short discussion (roughly 10–15
     sentences) addressing which of its recommended practices are compelling, which are not, which
     you already use and why, why researchers might not consistently adopt them, and which
     practices belong more to data analysis versus to software engineering.
  b. Skim a supplied paper's Method section for its main analysis steps (not its full detail), then
     examine the authors' accompanying public code repository. Without reading either closely,
     assess: can you quickly find where in the code the data was collected, cleaned, analyzed and
     plotted; what elements of the project's documentation, comments, organization, naming,
     workflow and data provenance are strong or weak; and whether you can tell what each file and
     block of code does without reading it in detail. Produce a short list of strengths and
     weaknesses to bring to the group discussion.
